description: We are an ambitious team from Bangladesh combining expertise in AI/ML, Large Language Models UI/UX design for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. To address the Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars challenge, we train custom AI models and LLMs on NASA’s planetary datasets—analyzing terrain, climate, and mineralogy to map Earth locations that mirror lunar and Martian environments.
summary:
Terra Analog, developed by Team Zenith, is an interactive web application that helps users investigate potential Earth analogs for lunar and Martian terrain. It compares NASA elevation data from the Moon's Shackleton rim and Mars's Arcadia Planitia with prepared Iceland windows or user-selected Earth locations where public data is available.

Each comparison covers a 5 x 5 km area on a 50 m processing grid. Users can explore linked 3D terrain views, inspect relative-height profiles and slope distributions, and compare measured terrain differences. Downloadable evidence packages preserve source links, processing methods, footprints, and checksums.

The project addresses the challenge by making terrain evidence accessible before Earth locations are proposed for further analog investigation. Its English and Bengali interfaces support education and exploratory research. All measurements come from deterministic code and traceable source data; missing information remains visible. Terra Analog provides a transparent foundation for further investigation, while validated analog rankings, ice analysis, and engineering safety assessment remain future work.
details:
Terra Analog turns planetary and Earth elevation datasets into an interactive workspace for investigating terrain similarities and differences. Developed by Team Zenith, it helps researchers, students, and educators examine evidence relevant to potential Earth analog locations.

The current application includes two planetary references: the Shackleton Site04 rim on the Moon and crater-bedform terrain in Arcadia Planitia on Mars. Users can compare either reference with three prepared Iceland areas or select an Earth location through place-name search, map clicks, or coordinates. Additional Earth terrain is processed on an explicit request where public data coverage is available.

Each landscape is represented by a 5 x 5 km footprint on a 50 m processing grid. The processing pipeline checks source integrity, transforms elevations into metric coordinate systems, and derives terrain measurements using deterministic calculations. Missing cells remain unavailable, and absolute elevations from different planetary vertical datums are not directly compared.

Users explore paired 3D surfaces with linked camera controls, slope colours, and shared vertical exaggeration. Interactive cross-sections reveal relative-height changes, while slope histograms and comparison tables describe differences in steepness, elevation variation, and low-slope area. Available ESA WorldCover data adds Earth land-cover context. English and Bengali interfaces broaden access, and source-derived 2D previews support devices where 3D rendering is unavailable.

NASA LRO/LOLA data provides the lunar reference, and NASA MRO/HiRISE data provides the Martian reference. Earth elevations come from PGC ArcticDEM and public Copernicus GLO-30 products. The application uses Python, FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, Rasterio, Shapely, and Matplotlib for processing and services; React, TypeScript, Three.js, and Leaflet power the interface and visualizations. The submission deployment uses Render.

The project's creative contribution is the connection between interactive exploration and traceable evidence. Users can move from a visual comparison to measured differences and download an evidence ZIP containing terrain records, graphs, geographic footprints, source metadata, method snapshots, and checksums.

Our intended impact is to make early terrain investigation more accessible and reproducible, support classroom learning, and help users formulate better questions for future field studies. Throughout development, we considered coordinate frames, processing scale, data coverage, source integrity, missing measurements, and the limitations of surface elevation models.

The current release is exploratory. It does not establish validated analog sites, calibrated similarity rankings, ice presence, or rover safety. Independent validation and effective-resolution assessment remain necessary before stronger scientific claims can be made.
